title: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
summary: How Genie learns a playable world from unlabelled video with a spatiotemporal tokenizer, 8 latent actions and a MaskGIT dynamics model, why rollouts drift, and how diffusion engines and metrics compare.
outcomes: Explain how a world model differs from a video model and why Genie needs latent actions
Compute token counts and full vs ST-factorized attention costs for a video clip
Trace how a VQ bottleneck of 8 codes turns frame pairs into controllable latent actions
Explain MaskGIT frame decoding and why autoregressive rollouts drift and how noise augmentation helps
Choose between FVD, delta PSNR and human studies to evaluate fidelity and controllability

lessons.title: World models, and why Genie learns one from unlabelled video

blocks.md: A classic game engine runs a loop: read the player's input, update the hidden game state with hand-written rules, then render that state to pixels. A **world model** replaces the rules and the renderer with a learned network. Given the frames so far and the player's actions, it samples the next frame:

blocks.caption: o are observations (frames), a are actions. Feeding each sampled frame back in as context turns the network into a playable simulator.

blocks.md: The idea is older than large video models. In *World Models* (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018) the agent has three parts: **V**, a variational autoencoder that compresses each frame into a 32-dimensional code $z_t$; **M**, a recurrent network with a mixture density output (MDN-RNN) that predicts $P(z_{t+1} \mid a_t, z_t, h_t)$; and **C**, a tiny linear controller. On CarRacing the controller had only 867 parameters and scored 906 plus or minus 21 over 100 trials, above the 900 that counts as solving the task.

The same paper trained a VizDoom agent entirely inside the model's own "dream" and transferred the policy back to the real game. **DreamerV3** (Hafner et al.) pushes this model-based reinforcement learning (RL) line much further: a recurrent state-space model encodes inputs into stochastic categorical latents, predicts rewards and episode ends, and an actor and critic learn from imagined rollouts of 16 steps. With one fixed configuration it handles over 150 tasks and was the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch without human data.

A learned world model is not the real environment. Ha and Schmidhuber found their agent discovered an *adversarial policy* that exploited flaws in M, doing well in the dream but not in reality. They raised a sampling temperature to make the dream noisier and harder to exploit. Every world model in this course shares this risk.

All of these models learn from transitions that include the action taken at each step, collected by interacting with the environment. That is the bottleneck Genie (Bruce et al., 2024) attacks. The Internet holds enormous amounts of gameplay video, but nobody recorded which buttons were pressed. Genie's authors filtered over 200,000 hours of public gaming video down to 30,000 hours of 2D platformer clips (6.8M clips of 16 s at 10 FPS, 160x90 pixels) and trained an 11B-parameter model on video alone.

blocks.title: From action-labelled world models to Genie

scenes.caption: A classic action-conditioned world model: frames plus the action logged at every step train a model of the next frame.
Internet video has no action log. Without actions the model can only predict a likely future, not a controllable one.
Genie adds a latent action model that looks at consecutive frames and infers which of 8 discrete codes best explains the change. The dynamics model is trained on those codes.
At play time the latent action model is thrown away (only its 8-entry codebook is kept). A person or agent picks an integer 0 to 7 each frame, like a button on an unfamiliar controller.

blocks.md: Genie has three learned parts, each covered in its own lesson: a **video tokenizer** that turns frames into discrete tokens, a **latent action model** (LAM) that discovers a small action vocabulary without labels, and a **dynamics model** that predicts the next frame's tokens from past tokens and an action. The paper's own comparison: world models need video plus actions and give frame-level control; video models need video plus text and give video-level control; Genie needs only video and gives frame-level control.

blocks.prompt: Genie was trained only on 2D platformer videos. What do you expect happens if you prompt it with a hand-drawn sketch or a real photo?
blocks.reveal: The paper shows it still produces game-like, controllable behaviour from such out-of-distribution prompts: text-to-image outputs, sketches and real photos all become playable, with a character that moves when you press a latent action. It even reproduces parallax, moving the foreground faster than the background. Large-scale video-only training is what made this breadth possible.

blocks.question: What does Genie learn from that a text-to-video model does not need, and what does it not need that classic world models do?
options: It needs only video, yet offers frame-by-frame control that video models lack
It needs action labels but not text, like classic world models
It needs text captions per frame instead of actions
It needs a hand-written game engine to generate training data
blocks.explain: Genie trains on unlabelled video only. Classic world models (Ha and Schmidhuber, Dreamer) need the action at each step; text-to-video models give control only at the level of the whole clip. Genie's latent actions give per-frame control without labels.

blocks.question: Ha and Schmidhuber's VizDoom agent scored well inside its dream but poorly in the real game. What is the most likely cause?
options: The controller had too few parameters to play Doom
The VAE compressed frames to 32 numbers, which is too few to see anything
The policy exploited errors in the learned model that do not exist in the real game
Dreams always run at a different frame rate than the game
blocks.explain: The paper calls this cheating the world model: the controller finds an adversarial policy that triggers the model's mistakes. Making the dream noisier (higher temperature) made such exploits harder. Any agent trained inside a learned simulator can overfit to its flaws.

lessons.title: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time

blocks.md: Recall from visual tokenizers: a VQ encoder maps each image patch to the index of its nearest codebook vector, so an image becomes a grid of integers. Genie's video tokenizer is a VQ-VAE with a **codebook of 1024 codes** (embedding size 32) and **patch size 4**, about 200M parameters. Its twist is that the encoder and decoder are spatiotemporal transformers, so the tokens for frame $t$ can carry information from all earlier frames $x_{1:t}$.

Toy clip: 16 RGB frames of 64x64 pixels, patch size 4.

- Each frame becomes a 16x16 grid: **256 tokens per frame**, so the clip is $16 \times 256 = 4096$ tokens.
- Raw pixels: $16 \times 64 \times 64 \times 3 = 196{,}608$ values, or 1,572,864 bits at 8 bits each.
- Each token indexes 1024 codes, so it costs $\log_2 1024 = 10$ bits: 40,960 bits in total, **38.4x smaller**.

Genie keeps one token grid per frame. Some video tokenizers also merge frames in time. As a stated toy assumption, merging every 4 frames would leave 4 x 256 = 1024 tokens (10,240 bits, 153.6x smaller).

blocks.title: Toy 16-frame 64x64 clip: what the tokenizer saves

scenes.caption: Size in kilobits. Pixels cost 1572.9 kb; one 10-bit token per 4x4 patch per frame costs 41.0 kb, which is what Genie-style per-frame tokens give.
Number of sequence positions the dynamics model must handle: 196,608 pixel values, 4096 tokens, or 1024 if frames were merged in time (toy assumption, not Genie's design).

blocks.md: 4096 tokens is still a lot for attention. In full attention every token attends to every other, so a clip of $T$ frames with $S$ tokens each costs $(TS)^2$ query-key pairs. Genie instead uses an **ST-transformer** in all three components: each block has a **spatial** attention layer (each token attends only to the $S$ tokens of its own frame), then a **temporal** layer (each token attends only to the same position in other frames, with a causal mask), then one feed-forward layer.

blocks.title: Who attends to whom: 3 frames x 4 tokens

scenes.caption: Full spatiotemporal attention: all 12 x 12 = 144 query-key pairs are computed. Rows are queries, columns are keys, ordered by frame (f) then patch position (p).
Spatial layer: a token sees only tokens in its own frame. Three 4 x 4 blocks, 48 pairs. This layer mixes information across the image.
Temporal layer with a causal mask: a token sees the same patch position in its own and earlier frames. 24 pairs. This layer carries motion and memory through time.
One ST block stacks both (value 2 marks a pair used by both layers, the diagonal). Two hops (spatial then temporal) still connect any token to any earlier one, at far lower cost.

blocks.caption: Pair counts per attention layer, ignoring the causal mask (which roughly halves the temporal term).

blocks.md: Worked example with $S = 256$ and $T = 16$: full attention needs $4096^2 = 16{,}777{,}216$ pairs. The spatial layer needs $16 \times 256^2 = 1{,}048{,}576$ and the temporal layer $256 \times 16^2 = 65{,}536$, for **1,114,112** in total, about **15.1x fewer**. With the causal mask the temporal layer drops to $256 \times 16 \times 17 / 2 = 34{,}816$ pairs.

blocks.title: Attention pairs vs number of frames

scenes.caption: With 256 tokens per frame, full attention grows with the square of the frame count. The ST total grows almost linearly because the spatial term dominates. At 16 frames: 16.8M vs 1.11M pairs.
At 64 frames the gap is 268M vs 5.2M pairs, a ratio of TS/(S+T) = 51.2. Longer memory is where factorization pays off most.
Larger frames (1024 tokens) push both curves up; the spatial term S squared T now dominates the ST cost even more, so resolution, not clip length, becomes the expensive axis.

blocks.md: In an ST-transformer the dominant cost, spatial attention, scales **linearly** with the number of frames instead of quadratically. That is what lets Genie use spatiotemporal context in the tokenizer, the latent action model and the dynamics model.

Does it help quality, not just cost? Genie's tokenizer ablation trained the same dynamics and action models on three tokenizers of similar size: a spatial-only ViT, C-ViViT (full space-time attention, from Phenaki) and their ST-ViViT. The ST version gave the best video quality (lowest FVD) and the best controllability, while C-ViViT used the most memory and tended to overfit.

scenes.caption: FVD, lower is better: 114.5, 272.7 and 81.4. Full space-time attention did not translate into better videos.
Memory in GB: 0.3, 1.6 and 0.9. ST-ViViT sits between the spatial-only and full-attention tokenizers.
Controllability (delta PSNR, higher is better, defined in lesson 3): 1.39, 1.37 and 1.66.

blocks.question: Keep S = 256 tokens per frame and double the clip from 16 to 32 frames. What happens to the attention pair counts?
options: Every term doubles, so the ratio stays at 15.1
Spatial pairs double to 2,097,152, temporal pairs quadruple to 262,144, full attention quadruples to 67,108,864
Spatial pairs quadruple and temporal pairs double
Nothing changes because attention is per frame
blocks.explain: Spatial is T S squared, linear in T. Temporal is S T squared, quadratic in T but small while T is much less than S. Full is (TS) squared. The ST total is 2,359,296, so the advantage grows to TS/(S+T) = 28.4x.

blocks.question: Why might a spatial-only tokenizer (one frame at a time) give worse controllability than ST-ViViT?
options: Its codebook is necessarily smaller
Spatial attention is more expensive than temporal attention
It uses a causal mask in space
It cannot encode information about motion between frames into the tokens
blocks.explain: A per-frame encoder sees no other frames, so its tokens carry no motion context. The ST tokenizer's causal temporal layers let each frame's tokens include what happened before, which helps the downstream models predict and control change.

lessons.title: Latent actions: a controller learned from unlabelled video

blocks.md: To make video controllable, each predicted frame should depend on the action taken at the previous frame. Internet videos lack those labels, so Genie learns **latent actions**. The latent action model has an encoder and a decoder. The encoder sees the past frames $x_{1:t}$ *and* the next frame $x_{t+1}$ and outputs a continuous latent action $\tilde a_t$. The decoder sees only the past frames and $\tilde a_t$ and must reconstruct $x_{t+1}$.

The trick is the bottleneck. $\tilde a_t$ is quantized with a VQ codebook of only $|A| = 8$ codes (embedding size 32). Since the decoder never sees the future frame, the code has to carry the most important change between past and future, and with only 8 choices it cannot smuggle in the whole next frame. Genie's LAM has about 300M parameters, works on raw pixels with patch size 16, and is trained jointly with the dynamics model.

blocks.title: Latent action model: training and inference

scenes.caption: The encoder sees both the past and the true next frame, so it knows what changed.
Its output is snapped to one of 8 codes. This tiny vocabulary is the bottleneck that forces each code to mean a consistent kind of change.
The decoder gets the history plus the code and must reconstruct the next frame. Its reconstruction loss is the only training signal for the LAM; the decoder exists for nothing else.
The same code (as a stop-gradient embedding) conditions the dynamics model during training.
At inference the encoder and decoder are discarded. A player picks an integer, it indexes the codebook, and the embedding drives the dynamics model.

blocks.md: A toy of the quantization step. Real codes are 32-dimensional and learned; here the codebook is 8 two-dimensional unit vectors so you can see the geometry. The encoder output for a frame pair is snapped to the nearest code by Euclidean distance.

blocks.title: Snapping a frame pair to one of 8 latent actions (toy 2D codebook)

scenes.caption: The codebook: 8 vectors. Their meaning is not designed; in a trained model each code ends up as some consistent change, such as move right or jump.
Frame pair A (character moves): encoder outputs (0.90, 0.35). Distances computed to all 8 codes; code 0 is nearest at 0.36, with code 1 close behind at 0.41.
Frame pair B (a different motion): encoder outputs (-0.15, -0.80). Code 6 wins clearly at 0.25. Distinct changes land on distinct codes.
Frame pair C (almost nothing moves): output (0.05, 0.08) sits near the centre, all distances 0.91 to 1.09, yet code 1 must still be chosen. Every transition is forced into one of 8 actions.

blocks.prompt: Why not give the LAM 1024 action codes, like the tokenizer, so it can describe changes more precisely?
blocks.reveal: Genie's appendix reports a benefit from more codes, but at the cost of reduced playability for human and AI agents. A person cannot learn the meaning of hundreds of buttons, and a wide bottleneck lets the code describe much more of the next frame's content rather than a small set of consistent controls. The paper picked $|A| = 8$ to permit human playability and enforce controllability.

blocks.md: Should the LAM read raw pixels or the tokenizer's tokens? Genie tried both (Table 2). With token input, FVD was slightly better on Platformers (38.8 vs 40.1) but much worse on Robotics (257.8 vs 136.4), and controllability was lower in both. The authors conclude that tokenization loses some motion information, so the LAM reads pixels.

Controllability is measured with $\Delta_t\mathrm{PSNR}$. Peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) compares two images in decibels; higher means closer. Generate frame $t$ twice from the same start: once with latent actions inferred from the real video ($\hat x_t$) and once with random latent actions ($\hat x'_t$). If actions matter, the random-action video should drift further from the truth. Genie reports $t = 4$.

Worked toy with pixels in [0, 1] (MAX = 1): if the inferred-action frame has MSE 0.004 against the truth, PSNR is $10\log_{10}(250) = 23.98$ dB. If the random-action frame has MSE 0.006, PSNR is 22.22 dB. So $\Delta_4\mathrm{PSNR} = 1.76$ dB, in the range Genie reports (1.91 for its pixel-input LAM on Platformers).

Do the codes mean anything? The authors found each latent action kept a consistent meaning across very different prompts, "akin to learning the buttons on a new controller". On robot videos, three latent actions each produced one consistent motion (down, up and left) from three different starting frames. In CoinRun, a frozen LAM labelled expert videos with latent actions, a policy learned to predict them, and a small labelled set mapped latent to real actions; this matched an oracle behavioural cloning agent with as few as 200 expert samples.

blocks.question: A model's $\Delta_t\mathrm{PSNR}$ is close to 0. What does that tell you?
options: The video quality is very high
The tokenizer failed to reconstruct frames
The model is perfectly controllable
Random actions produce frames about as close to the truth as inferred actions, so the actions barely control the output
blocks.explain: If swapping the true latent actions for random ones does not change how far the prediction lands from the real frame, the model is mostly ignoring the action input. High controllability shows up as a large positive gap.

blocks.question: Which part of the latent action model is still used when a person plays Genie?
options: The encoder, to infer actions from the player's screen
The decoder, to render each frame
Only the VQ codebook, indexed by the integer the player chooses
Nothing; the dynamics model takes raw keyboard codes
blocks.explain: Apart from the VQ codebook, the entire LAM is discarded at inference. The player's integer in [0, 8) selects a code vector, whose embedding conditions the dynamics model.

lessons.title: The dynamics model: next-frame tokens with MaskGIT

blocks.md: The **dynamics model** is a decoder-only MaskGIT transformer (built from ST blocks). At each step it reads the tokens of all earlier frames $z_{1:t-1}$ and the latent actions $\tilde a_{1:t-1}$ and predicts the token grid of the next frame $\hat z_t$. Because the temporal attention is causal, one forward pass over a 16-frame training clip produces predictions for frames 2 to 16 at once, trained with cross-entropy against the real tokens.

Two details from the paper matter. First, actions enter as **additive embeddings** on the tokens rather than being concatenated as an extra token; the authors found this improved controllability. Second, during training the input tokens are randomly masked with a Bernoulli rate drawn uniformly between 0.5 and 1, so the model practises filling in heavily masked frames, which is exactly what it does when generating.

Recall MaskGIT (Chang et al., 2022): instead of predicting tokens one by one in raster order, start with every token of the frame masked. Each iteration predicts all masked tokens in parallel, keeps the most confident ones, and re-masks the rest. The number left masked after iteration $t$ of $T_{\text{it}}$ follows a schedule; the cosine schedule worked best in the MaskGIT ablations.

blocks.caption: N is the number of tokens per frame. Few tokens are committed early, when the model knows little; more are committed once context has filled in.

blocks.title: Cosine unmasking of one 256-token frame in 8 iterations

scenes.caption: Our toy frame has 16 x 16 = 256 tokens. Before iteration 1 every token is masked.
Early iterations are cautious: only 4 tokens kept after iteration 1, then 15 and 24. These are the positions the model is most confident about, such as static background.
Once context is filled in, each step commits more: 31, 39, 45, 48. Every iteration is one full forward pass of the dynamics model.
Iteration 8 commits the last 50 tokens. 8 passes generated 256 tokens; token-by-token decoding would need 256 passes. Genie itself uses 25 MaskGIT steps per frame with temperature 2.
A single prompt image (a sketch, a photo, a generated image) is encoded into the first token grid z1.
The player chooses latent action a1, an integer in 0 to 7. The dynamics model runs 25 MaskGIT iterations to produce z2.
The new tokens are decoded back into pixels and shown to the player.
The loop repeats. z2 joins the context, which is how predictions feed back in. Changing the actions from the same start yields a different trajectory.

blocks.code:
def play(prompt_image, choose_action, n_frames, steps=25, temp=2.0):
    z = [tokenizer.encode(prompt_image)]        # 1 x H' x W' token grid
    a = []
    for t in range(1, n_frames):
        a.append(lam_codebook[choose_action()])  # integer 0..7 -> embedding
        z_next = all_masked_like(z[0])
        for i in range(steps):                   # MaskGIT refinement
            logits = dynamics(z + [z_next], a)   # ST-transformer, causal in time
            z_next = keep_most_confident(logits, z_next, step=i, temp=temp)
        z.append(z_next)
        yield tokenizer.decode(z)[-1]            # pixels for the new frame
blocks.caption: Simplified inference loop (pseudocode; helper names are illustrative). The real model also limits context to 16 frames.

blocks.md: Scale: the scaling study trained dynamics models from 40M to 2.7B parameters, and final training loss fell consistently with size; larger batches also helped. The final Genie dynamics model has 10.1B parameters, trained with batch size 512 for 125k steps on 256 TPUv5p, for 10.7B parameters in total with the tokenizer and LAM, trained on 942B tokens.

Generating a frame is not one forward pass. Each frame costs a full MaskGIT loop (25 passes in Genie) over a context that grows with every frame. The paper's own limitations: Genie runs at around 1 FPS and is limited to 16 frames of memory.

blocks.question: Why does Genie train the dynamics model with masking rates drawn between 0.5 and 1 rather than always masking just the last frame completely?
options: To make training cheaper by skipping tokens
Because MaskGIT decoding starts from a heavily masked frame and refines partially filled ones, so training must cover many masking levels
To hide the latent actions from the model
To make the tokenizer's codebook smaller
blocks.explain: At inference each frame goes from fully masked to fully filled through intermediate states. Training on a range of masking rates teaches the model to predict masked tokens from the partial context it will see at every iteration.

blocks.question: Generating 16 frames from one prompt frame with 25 MaskGIT steps per frame needs how many dynamics forward passes?
blocks.explain: The prompt frame is given, so 15 new frames are generated, each needing 25 passes: 15 x 25 = 375. This sequential cost is a big reason the original Genie ran near 1 FPS.

lessons.title: Rollout drift and diffusion game engines

blocks.md: Training uses **teacher forcing**: the context frames are real. Playing uses **autoregressive** rollout: the context is the model's own earlier outputs. Small mistakes in frame 5 become inputs for frame 6, and the model was never trained on its own mistakes. GameNGen (Valevski et al.) shows this directly: without a fix, quality degrades fast after 20 to 30 steps.

A simplified model makes the dynamics visible. Let $e_t$ be the error at step $t$. Each step adds a fresh error $\epsilon$, and existing error is multiplied by a factor $\rho$: $\rho > 1$ means the model amplifies its own mistakes, $\rho < 1$ means it partially corrects them.

blocks.caption: A toy linear model of error accumulation, not a fitted curve from any paper.

blocks.prompt: With per-step error 0.02, compare amplification 1.07 and correction 0.91. Roughly how big is the error after 30 frames in each case?
blocks.reveal: With $\rho = 1.07$: $0.02 \times (1.07^{30} - 1)/0.07 = 1.89$, almost 100 times the one-step error and still growing exponentially. With $\rho = 0.91$: $0.209$, close to its ceiling $0.02/0.09 = 0.222$. The per-step error is the same; what decides long rollouts is whether errors are amplified or damped.

scenes.caption: rho = 1.07, eps = 0.02: error is 0.28 after 10 frames and 1.89 after 30. Teacher-forced metrics would only ever show the flat 0.02 line.
Halving the per-step error (eps = 0.01) only halves the curve, to 0.94 at frame 30. A better one-step model delays drift but does not stop it.
Make the model correct its errors (rho = 0.91): error levels off near eps/(1 - rho) = 0.22 (0.209 at frame 30). This is the goal of noise augmentation.

blocks.md: GameNGen's fix is **noise augmentation**. It repurposes Stable Diffusion v1.4 as a next-frame model for DOOM: past frames are encoded into latents and concatenated to the noisy latent channels, and each key press is embedded as a token that replaces the text cross-attention. During training, the context latents are corrupted with Gaussian noise of a random level (up to 0.7, in 10 buckets), and the level is given to the model. The network learns to repair imperfect context, which is what it will see in its own rollouts.

GameNGen's training data came from a PPO agent learning to play, recorded throughout training (70M examples). It conditions on the last 64 frames and actions, a little over 3 seconds. Results from the paper: next-frame PSNR 29.43 (similar to lossy JPEG at quality 20 to 30) and FVD 114.02 over 16 frames. Human raters picked the real game only 58% to 60% of the time on short clips, and 50% for clips taken after 5 to 10 minutes of generation.

blocks.title: GameNGen per-frame latency on one TPU-v5

scenes.caption: The paper measures 10 ms per denoiser step and 10 ms for the auto-encoder. With 4 DDIM steps a frame costs 50 ms, so the engine runs at 20 frames per second.
A distilled one-step model needs 20 ms, or 50 FPS, but the paper reports some quality cost, so the main results use 4 undistilled steps (which scored about the same as 20 or more).

blocks.md: **DIAMOND** (Alonso et al., 2024) is a diffusion world model used to train RL agents. The authors argue that discrete latent tokens can drop small visual details that matter for control, such as an enemy rendered as a reward. Built on the EDM diffusion formulation, it stayed stable even with very few denoising steps where a DDPM version suffered compounding error. It uses 3 denoising steps at 64x64 and reached a mean human-normalized score of 1.46 on Atari 100k, then the best for agents trained entirely in a world model.

DIAMOND also scaled to Counter-Strike: Global Offensive: a 381M-parameter model trained on 87 hours of human gameplay of one map runs at about 10 Hz on an RTX 3090. The authors note its limited memory: looking at a wall can make it forget the current state and invent a new weapon or area.

Two routes to the next frame: **discrete tokens plus a masked transformer** (Genie) and **continuous latents plus diffusion** (GameNGen, DIAMOND, and per its blog post, Genie 2). Both are autoregressive over frames, so both must fight drift and limited memory.

blocks.question: GameNGen without noise augmentation degrades after about 20 to 30 frames even though its single-frame quality is good. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Train longer with teacher forcing on clean context frames
Use more DDIM sampling steps per frame
Corrupt the context frames with noise during training and tell the model the noise level
Increase the output resolution
blocks.explain: The cause is a train and test mismatch: clean context in training, imperfect self-generated context in play. Noise augmentation trains the model to correct damaged context, the toy equivalent of pushing rho below 1. More sampling steps improve each frame but do not teach correction.

blocks.question: In DIAMOND's Boxing experiments, one denoising step gave a blurry opponent but three steps gave a crisp one. Why?
options: One step is not enough compute to render any sprite
The opponent's moves are uncertain, so a single step averages possible futures; iterating commits to one mode
The agent's own player is also blurry for the same reason
Blur is caused by the auto-encoder, not the denoiser
blocks.explain: A one-step denoiser trained with an L2 loss outputs the mean of all plausible next frames, which blurs when the future is multimodal. The agent's own player stayed sharp because its action is known to the model. Multi-step sampling drives the sample toward one mode.

lessons.title: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next

blocks.md: How do you score a world model? Per-frame PSNR against the real video punishes any plausible future that differs from the one recorded; GameNGen notes its rollouts diverge from ground truth mostly through small differences in movement speed. So papers report distribution-level video quality, controllability, and human judgements.

**Fréchet Video Distance (FVD)** (Unterthiner et al.) runs real and generated clips through an I3D network (a 3D convolutional video classifier trained on the Kinetics dataset), fits a Gaussian to each set of feature vectors, and measures the Fréchet distance between the two Gaussians. Lower is better. Because the features come from whole clips, FVD rewards both frame quality and plausible motion.

blocks.caption: mu and Sigma are the mean and covariance of I3D features for real (r) and generated (g) clips.

blocks.md: One-dimensional toy: real features with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, generated with mean 0.3 and standard deviation 0.8. The formula reduces to $(\mu_r - \mu_g)^2 + (\sigma_r - \sigma_g)^2 = 0.09 + 0.04 = 0.13$. A shifted mean and a too-narrow spread (less diversity) both add distance.

FVD alone cannot tell whether a model listens to actions. A model that ignores the controls but produces realistic clips can score well. That is why Genie pairs FVD with delta PSNR, and why its pixel-input LAM was chosen despite a slightly worse Platformers FVD (40.1 vs 38.8): its controllability was much higher (1.91 vs 1.33).

blocks.title: GameNGen human study: how often raters picked the real game

scenes.caption: Raters saw the real game and the simulation side by side and had to pick the real one. 58% and 60% is only slightly better than the 50% of guessing.

After 5 to 10 minutes of autoregressive play, raters were at chance (50%). The authors add that they themselves, knowing the simulation's flaws, could often spot it within seconds of actually playing, so short-clip studies flatter interactive quality.

blocks.md: **Genie 2** (Google DeepMind blog) moves to rich 3D worlds from a single prompt image, played with keyboard and mouse. The blog describes it as an autoregressive latent diffusion model: an autoencoder produces latent frames, a large transformer dynamics model with a causal mask predicts them, and classifier-free guidance improves action controllability. It can keep a world consistent for up to a minute (most shown examples last 10 to 20 s) and can re-render parts of the scene that went out of view. A distilled version plays in real time at reduced quality.

**Genie 3** (Google DeepMind blog) generates worlds from a text prompt that can be navigated in real time at 24 frames per second and 720p, staying consistent for a few minutes, with visual memory reaching back about one minute. It adds *promptable world events*: text that changes the world mid-session, such as the weather or new objects. The blog stresses that this consistency is emergent, not built on an explicit 3D representation such as NeRFs or Gaussian splatting, and lists limitations: a constrained action space, modelling multiple interacting agents, geographic accuracy for real places, text rendering, and sessions of minutes rather than hours.

scenes.caption: Frames per second as each source states it: Genie about 1, GameNGen 20 on one TPU, DIAMOND's CS:GO model about 10 on an RTX 3090, Genie 3 24 in real time. Hardware and resolution differ, so this is not a benchmark.

blocks.md: A video world model is three choices: how frames become latents (VQ tokens or continuous), how actions enter (logged, learned latent codes, or text), and how the next frame is sampled (masked token decoding or diffusion). All of them pay for autoregression with drift and finite memory, and they are judged on fidelity (FVD, human studies) and on control (delta PSNR).

blocks.question: You train two models on the same data. Model X has FVD 80 and delta PSNR 0.1; model Y has FVD 90 and delta PSNR 1.8. You want a playable environment. Which do you pick and why?
options: X, because lower FVD always means a better world model
Neither, FVD under 100 means both are unusable
Y, because X's actions barely change its output, so it is a good video model but a poor interactive one
X, because delta PSNR only matters for robotics
blocks.explain: A world model must respond to actions. X generates slightly more realistic clips but random actions make almost no difference to its output. Y trades a little fidelity for strong control, the same tradeoff Genie made when choosing a pixel-input LAM.

blocks.question: A team wants to train an RL agent for an Atari game cheaply using imagined experience, and they can collect actions and rewards by playing. Which approach fits best?
options: A model-based RL world model trained on their own action-labelled transitions, such as DreamerV3 or DIAMOND
A Genie-style model trained on unlabelled internet video, since labels are unnecessary
A text-to-video model prompted with the game's name
No world model: imagined experience cannot train agents
blocks.explain: When actions and rewards are available, action-conditioned world models built for RL (DreamerV3's latent imagination, DIAMOND's diffusion model with an Atari 100k mean HNS of 1.46) are the direct fit. Genie's latent actions solve a different problem: learning control from video with no labels.
